strengths: Identifies and formalizes a practically relevant but understudied problem: multi-objective routing on multigraphs, where parallel edges with distinct attributes must be selected, and extends learning-based routing beyond simple Euclidean graphs.

Proposes two complementary neural architectures: an edge-based autoregressive solver (GMS-EB) that constructs routes directly on the multigraph, and a dual-head solver (GMS-DH) that learns to prune parallel edges before node-based routing. Both use preference-conditioned hypernetworks for multi-objective optimization.
Provides an extensive empirical study across MOTSP, MOCVRP, MGMOTSP, and MGMOTSPTW, multiple instance sizes, asymmetric and multigraph distributions, zero-shot generalization, and ablations.

Reports strong performance relative to the neural baseline (MBM) and MOEAs on several tasks, especially multigraph and time-window settings, while maintaining practical inference times compared with LKH3 in many cases.

Appendix includes substantial additional detail on problem definitions, data distributions, architectures, training curriculum, baseline setups, and complementary numerical results, supporting reproducibility to a reasonable extent.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is moderate: the approach largely combines existing components (GREAT encoder, multi-pointer decoder, hypernetworks, POMO/REINFORCE), with the main contribution being the new problem setting and adaptation rather than a fundamentally new learning mechanism.

On the main MOTSP and MGMOTSP benchmarks, the methods still lag behind LKH3, and no exact multi-objective solver is available for comparison; thus claims of competitiveness are relative to weaker neural/MOEA baselines in some cases.

MOCVRP evaluation lacks strong single-objective/exact baselines such as LKH3 or OR-Tools, so the reported best/zero-gap results are only relative to the included methods and may overstate absolute solution quality.

The neural multi-objective comparison is limited mainly to a self-designed MBM baseline. Other recent neural multi-objective combinatorial optimization methods are not adapted or compared against in the main multigraph/asymmetric setting.

GMS-DH selection-head training relies on a biased approximation of the optimal tour via the maximum over sampled tours, and the edge selection cannot depend on the evolving partial tour, which may limit optimality and lacks theoretical guarantees.

Training times for GMS-EB and GMS-DH are substantial, and no public code release is mentioned; several important implementation details (inference scalarization, HV normalization, baseline tuning) are relegated to the appendix, which may hinder full reproducibility.

Some empirical claims could be stated more cautiously: the models are not uniformly best, and in several main tables LKH3 remains clearly superior, while the strongest gains appear on problem variants where strong exact or heuristic MO baselines are unavailable.

strengths: The paper addresses an underexplored and practically relevant problem: multi-objective routing on multigraphs, where multiple edges with distinct attributes exist between node pairs.

It proposes two GNN-based solvers, GMS-EB (edge-based autoregressive construction) and GMS-DH (dual-head learned pruning followed by routing), extending existing neural combinatorial optimization components to the multigraph setting.
The empirical study is broad: it covers MOTSP, MOCVRP, MGMOTSP, and MGMOTSPTW across multiple distributions (TMAT, XASY, FLEX, FIX), instance sizes, and zero-shot generalization.

The results show that GMS-EB generally outperforms the neural baseline and MOEAs, while GMS-DH offers faster inference; the learned pruning in GMS-DH shows particular value on the harder MGMOTSPTW problem.
The paper provides substantial reproducibility details in the appendix, including architecture components, training schedules, hyperparameters, and hardware.
The use of hypervolume, runtime, ablations, and comparisons to LKH/OR-Tools/MOEAs gives a reasonably thorough empirical picture.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is limited: the core components (GREAT encoder, multi-pointer decoder, POMO, hypernetwork conditioning, MatNet baseline) are existing, and the main contribution is an adaptation/combination for multigraph edge selection rather than a fundamentally new learning approach.

The evaluation lacks comparisons to recent neural multi-objective routing methods (e.g., Lin et al. 2022 and successors) on asymmetric or simple-graph MOTSP, relying instead on a custom MatNet-based baseline and classical/MOEA baselines; this weakens the claim of broad applicability and state-of-the-art positioning.
Experiments are restricted to bi-objective problems (m=2), despite the paper framing the work as general multi-objective routing; scalability to three or more objectives is not demonstrated.

The GMS-DH training procedure relies on ad hoc approximations, including independent edge-selection factorization across node pairs and a max-over-sampled-tours reward estimator, with no theoretical guarantees; the selection head also cannot adapt edge choices to the partial tour context, as the authors acknowledge.
GMS-EB scales poorly (O(MN^4)), and GMS-DH loses tour-context-dependent edge selection, so both methods have significant practical limitations that are only briefly discussed.

Baseline comparisons are somewhat uneven: LKH/OR-Tools are applied via scalarization, MOEAs are not well tuned for large asymmetric instances, and runtime comparisons mix GPU neural inference with parallelized CPU baselines.

The theoretical contribution is thin: Proposition 1 is a straightforward observation for linear scalarization only, and the paper does not provide deeper analysis of the dual-head training or pruning approximation.

Training times for GMS are very high (e.g., GMS-EB requires 1.7 hours per epoch for 50-node multigraphs), which raises practical reproducibility and scalability concerns beyond the brief acknowledgement in the appendix.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and underexplored problem: multi-objective routing on multigraphs, where edge selection and node selection must be made jointly, with clear real-world relevance.

Proposes two non-trivial GNN-based architectures, GMS-EB and GMS-DH, combining edge-based autoregressive decoding, preference-conditioned hypernetworks, learned multigraph pruning, and node-based routing.

Provides an extensive empirical study across multiple routing problems (MOTSP, MOCVRP, MGMOTSP, MGMOTSPTW), distributions (TMAT, XASY, FLEXx, FIXx), instance sizes (20-200), and zero-shot generalization settings.
Demonstrates strong practical performance: GMS-EB often closes much of the gap to LKH and performs especially well on MOCVRP and MGMOTSPTW, while GMS-DH offers a favorable speed/quality trade-off.
Includes useful ablations comparing learned edge selection, simple pruning, and pre-pruning, showing that learned selection can help on problems where a priori pruning is not sound.

Provides detailed architecture and training descriptions in appendices, including curriculum learning, model sizes, hardware, and runtime information, supporting reproducibility to a reasonable extent.
The scalarization discussion and Proposition 1 help clarify when multigraph pruning is exact and when learned edge selection is more appropriate.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate: the core components (GREAT encoder, multi-pointer decoder, POMO, hypernetworks, MatNet baseline) are largely adapted from prior work, with the main contribution being a thoughtful architectural combination for a new setting.

GMS-DH's edge-selection head prunes parallel edges independently for each node pair before routing, so the selected edge cannot depend on the partial tour or route context. This can be suboptimal for non-additive objectives such as time-window violations or Chebyshev scalarizations, a limitation acknowledged but not fully addressed.

The dual-head training relies on approximating the optimal tour for the selection head by max over K2 sampled tours, which is an optimistic, biased estimator and lacks theoretical convergence or stability analysis.

The manuscript does not clearly specify how the ideal point z_i^* in the Chebyshev reward is computed. This is important for training and reproducibility, especially for MOCVRP and MGMOTSPTW where ideal values are not trivial.

Baselines relying on scalarization (LKH, OR-Tools) are primarily used with linear scalarization, which cannot recover non-supported Pareto-optimal points. This may understate their performance relative to neural models trained with Chebyshev rewards and slightly biases the HV comparison.

Experimental reporting lacks confidence intervals or statistical significance tests across the 200 test instances, making it difficult to assess whether small differences between methods are meaningful.

The comparison to recent neural multi-objective routing methods is limited. Although the authors argue existing methods are Euclidean-specific or problem-specific, a more explicit discussion or adapted comparison would strengthen the positioning.

Some claims about the importance of avoiding pre-pruning are not fully isolated: GMS-DH PP's poor performance may also be influenced by Chebyshev-vs-linear reward mismatch, re-encoding cost, and training distribution, rather than solely by pre-pruning being unsuitable.

strengths: Addresses a novel and practically relevant problem: learning-based multi-objective routing on multigraphs, where multiple parallel edges with different attributes exist between node pairs.

Proposes two complementary GNN-based methods: GMS-EB, an edge-based autoregressive model that directly constructs tours on the multigraph, and GMS-DH, a dual-head model that first learns to prune the multigraph and then performs node-based routing.

Methodologically combines suitable components such as GREAT-style edge embeddings, preference-conditioned multi-pointer decoders, hypernetworks, POMO-style sampling, and multi-objective REINFORCE in a reasonable way.

Provides an extensive empirical study across multiple problems (MOTSP, MOCVRP, MGMOTSP, MGMOCVRP, MGMOTSPTW), distributions (TMAT, XASY, FLEX/FIX), graph sizes, zero-shot generalization, and tri-objective settings.
Reports competitive results against strong heuristics, MOEAs, and neural baselines, with both models often outperforming neural baselines and occasionally approaching LKH/HGS.
Analyzes the trade-off between the more expressive but slower GMS-EB and the more scalable GMS-DH, including runtime and memory considerations.
Includes substantial implementation details, hyperparameters, training curricula, encoder/decoder descriptions, and additional ablations in the appendix.
weaknesses: The novelty is mostly architectural/application-driven: the paper adapts existing components (GREAT, multi-pointer decoders, hypernetworks, POMO) to the multigraph setting rather than introducing fundamentally new learning or optimization theory.
Theoretical contribution is limited; Proposition 1 is simple, its proof is omitted, and the learned pruning approach in GMS-DH lacks theoretical guarantees or error analysis.
The empirical evaluation does not report statistical significance, confidence intervals, or variance across runs, making some small hypervolume differences difficult to interpret.

Recent neural multi-objective combinatorial optimization baselines such as PMOCO/NHDE/POCCO are not empirically compared, even where adaptations might be possible; comparisons rely mainly on MBM and naive extensions.

The GMS-DH edge-selection decoder is non-autoregressive and cannot condition the pruned edge on the partial route, which limits its suitability for problems where edge choice depends on route context, as acknowledged by the authors.
The training of the GMS-DH selection head approximates the optimal tour by the maximum over sampled tours, which may introduce bias and sensitivity to K1/K2 without a clear theoretical justification.
No code or model release is mentioned, which weakens reproducibility despite the detailed appendix.

The explanation for why GMS-DH with pre-pruning underperforms is somewhat speculative, especially because linear scalarization pruning can be exact for additive objectives under the stated conditions.

strengths: Addresses a practically relevant and under-explored problem: multi-objective routing on multigraphs and asymmetric graphs, where existing neural routing methods are largely inapplicable without modification.

Proposes two concrete GNN-based architectures: an edge-based autoregressive solver operating directly on the multigraph and a dual-head solver combining learned non-autoregressive pruning with autoregressive routing.
The empirical study is broad, covering multiple routing problems, distributions, instance sizes, zero-shot generalization, and tri-objective settings in the appendix.
The dual-head NAR+AR design is technically interesting, and the paper demonstrates competitive performance among neural baselines on several multigraph settings.
The manuscript is generally well organized, with substantial implementation details and additional experiments in the appendices.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is limited: the proposed models largely combine existing components, including GREAT, POMO, multi-pointer decoders, hypernetworks, and scalarization-based multi-objective training. Being the first to apply such components to multigraph routing is a useful but incremental contribution.

The central claim that explicit multigraph-aware design is necessary is not convincingly supported. Proposition 1 shows exact pruning is possible under linear scalarization for MGMOTSP, and the post-encoder simple-pruning ablation performs similarly to the learned selection head on MGMOTSP, undermining the necessity of the learned pruning component in the main benchmark.

The GMS-DH pre-pruning variant performs poorly even though Proposition 1 suggests exact pruning should preserve the scalarized optimum. The explanation given, a vague distribution shift, is not rigorously investigated and reads as an implementation/training issue rather than a fundamental limitation of pruning.

The reported performance is not competitive with strong classical heuristics. LKH clearly dominates on MOTSP and MGMOTSP, while HGS dominates on MGMOCVRP. The text emphasizes competitive performance, but the tables exclude LKH/HGS from the bold comparison and do not adequately contextualize the substantial remaining gaps.

Scalability remains a serious weakness. GMS-EB scales poorly as O(MN^4), is very slow to train, and is evaluated only on relatively small instances. GMS-DH is faster but generally weaker, so the paper does not deliver a scalable and high-quality solver.

The evaluation lacks statistical rigor: no random seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported. Hypervolume reference points appear arbitrary and vary across distributions, making comparisons harder to interpret.

The experimental positioning is incomplete. Recent multi-objective neural solvers are not adapted or compared, and key neural baselines are limited to MBM/GRBM/GOBM. The main text only shows the best MOEA per scenario, with the rest relegated to appendices.

The training algorithm for GMS-DH is complex but under-analyzed. The selection-head reward approximates the optimal tour by a maximum over sampled tours, which is biased and high-variance, yet no theoretical justification or sensitivity analysis is provided. The use of curriculum learning and encoder freezing appears ad hoc.

Reproducibility is not sufficiently demonstrated. No code is mentioned, and important details such as reward normalization, Chebyshev ideal-point selection, and exact training schedules are either unclear or scattered across appendices.

Several claims are stronger than the evidence. The paper repeatedly suggests its multigraph-aware solvers are preferable to pruning, but the strongest supporting benchmark for this claim, MGMOTSPTW, considers only one instance size and does not provide a comprehensive picture.

strengths: Introduces the first learning-based solvers for multi-objective routing on multigraphs, addressing a practically relevant gap in neural combinatorial optimization.

Proposes two complementary GNN-based architectures with clear trade-offs: edge-based GMS-EB works directly on the multigraph, while dual-head GMS-DH learns to prune parallel edges before node-based routing and scales better.

Provides a broad empirical evaluation across multiple routing problems (MOTSP, MOCVRP, MGMOTSP, MGMOCVRP, MGMOTSPTW), graph distributions (TMAT, XASY, FLEX, FIX), sizes, zero-shot settings, and bi-/tri-objective variants.
Compares against strong baselines including LKH, OR-Tools, HGS, multiple MOEAs, and a neural MatNet-based baseline, with ablations isolating the benefit of learned pruning over pre-pruning.
The proposed methods are competitive or best-in-class in several settings, especially MOCVRP and MGMOTSPTW, and GMS-DH offers substantially faster inference than GMS-EB.
Reproducibility appears good: detailed architecture descriptions, training algorithms, hyperparameters, distributions, evaluation metrics, and hardware are provided in the appendices.
weaknesses: On several core benchmarks such as MOTSP, MGMOTSP, and MGMOCVRP, specialized classical heuristics like LKH and HGS still achieve higher hypervolume, so practical superiority is not fully established.

The evaluation relies on a finite preference grid (101 preferences) and hypervolume with chosen reference points; there is limited statistical significance testing or sensitivity analysis for Pareto-front quality.

GMS-EB has high scaling complexity and long training/inference times, while GMS-DH prunes edges non-autoregressively without tour context and approximates the optimal tour using sampled rollouts, which may introduce bias.

Several components are adapted from existing work (GREAT, multi-pointer decoder, hypernetworks, POMO, multi-objective REINFORCE); the core novelty lies mainly in the multigraph-specific decoder designs and their composition.
Timing comparisons between GPU-based neural methods and CPU-parallel classical heuristics are not fully apples-to-apples, and wall-clock advantages should be interpreted cautiously.
The study focuses on synthetic multigraph distributions and relatively small numbers of parallel edges; real-world multigraph constraints and larger edge-multiplicity regimes remain underexplored.
